notes.meaning: The Lord gave fresh instructions to Moses as Israel traveled near the edge of the desert. God spoke out of the pillar of cloud that led the people, showing that He was guiding every step of their journey.

God commanded the people to change direction and set up camp right beside the sea. Instead of taking the direct road out of Egypt, they were told to camp between the water and the mountains. God deliberately led them into a spot where they had no human way out.

The Lord explained that Pharaoh would think the Israelites had lost their way and were trapped by the wilderness. By turning south toward the sea, Israel appeared confused and helpless to Egyptian observers. God arranged this situation to lure Pharaoh into chasing them.

God stated that He would harden Pharaoh's stubborn heart so the king would pursue Israel. Through the defeat of Egypt's army, the Lord planned to show His power and prove to everyone that He alone is the true God. The Israelites obeyed God's command and set up camp by the sea.

When news reached Pharaoh that the Israelites had left for good, he and his leaders regretted letting them go. The terror of the ten plagues had passed, and greed made them grieve the loss of an entire nation of free slave workers. They decided to undo their decision and drag the people back.

Pharaoh prepared his royal war chariot and ordered his army to march. Egyptian kings usually led their soldiers in person to ensure victory and show their royal authority. His quick mobilization showed how determined he was to punish the Hebrews.

The king gathered six hundred of Egypt's elite chariots along with every other war chariot he could find. Chariots were the most feared military weapon of that era, carrying skilled drivers and armed warriors. Against an unarmed crowd of former slaves, this was a terrifying force.

The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart to make him chase after the Hebrews. Israel had marched out of Egypt with confidence and high spirits, thinking their struggles were finished. They did not expect Pharaoh to attack them after urging them to leave.

The Egyptian army, including all of Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and cavalry, caught up with Israel. The Israelites were resting by the water near Pi-hahiroth when the dust of the approaching army appeared. With the sea in front and soldiers behind, they were completely trapped.

As Pharaoh's forces closed in, the Israelites looked up and were gripped by terror. Because they had no weapons and carried their children and belongings, they had no way to defend themselves. In their panic, they cried out to the Lord for rescue.

The people turned on Moses with biting sarcasm, asking if he brought them to die in the desert because Egypt lacked graves. Egypt was known throughout the world for its massive tombs and cemeteries, which made their words especially sharp. In a single moment of fear, they forgot how God had protected them.

The crowd insisted they had warned Moses back in Egypt to leave them alone in their slavery. They argued that serving Egyptian masters was better than dying out in the wilderness. When fear took over, they preferred familiar bondage over the risk of trusting God.

Moses urged the frightened crowd not to panic, but to stand firm and watch God work. He promised that the Lord would save them that very day, meaning He would rescue their lives from destruction. He told them that the Egyptian army they saw would never threaten them again.

Moses declared that the Lord would do all the fighting, while the people only needed to stay quiet and still. They did not have to swing a sword or devise an escape plan, because God alone would defeat the enemy. When people face impossible odds, God calls them to rest in His power.

The Lord told Moses to stop crying out in prayer and command the people to march forward. Moses had been praying earnestly in his heart, but God showed him that the time for praying had passed and the time for action had come. True faith must step forward even before the path appears open.

God directed Moses to raise his shepherd's staff and stretch his hand over the water to split the sea. This action would open a dry road right through the middle of the deep waters for Israel to cross. The staff held no magic of its own, but God used it to confirm Moses as His chosen leader.

The Lord announced that He would make the Egyptians so reckless that they would march right into the seabed after Israel. Their blind hatred would lead them straight into their own destruction. Through this event, God would show His supreme majesty over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his riders.

God repeated that the Egyptians would finally learn that He is the one true Lord when He defeated their army. The overthrow of Pharaoh's forces would prove that Egyptian gods were powerless before the God of Israel. Those remaining behind in Egypt would hear the news and know God's power.

The angel of God and the pillar of cloud moved from the front of the Israelite camp to the rear. Israel did not need a guide in front while the sea was opening, but they urgently needed a shield behind them. God placed Himself directly between His people and the army that wanted to destroy them.

The pillar stood between the two camps all through the night, acting as a wall between them. It cast thick darkness over the Egyptians so they could not see, while giving bright light to Israel so they could get ready to move. Because of this divine barrier, the enemies could not touch Israel.

Moses stretched his hand over the water, and the Lord drove the sea back using a powerful east wind that blew all night long. The water split in two, turning the wet sea bottom into firm, dry ground. God used the wind as His tool to accomplish this mighty miracle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that a strong wind over a shallow, marshy lake caused a natural drop in water levels, rather than a miraculous division into tall walls of water.

notes.meaning: The Israelites walked straight into the sea bed on dry ground, flanked by walls of water on their right and left. Stepping between towering walls of water required strong faith, but God kept the waters held back. A huge multitude of men, women, children, and livestock crossed safely without sinking in mud.

Pharaoh's cavalry and chariots charged into the dry sea bed in hot pursuit of the Israelites. In the darkness and the fury of the chase, they failed to realize the deadly danger of entering a parted sea. They foolishly assumed that a path opened for God's people was just as safe for them.

Just before dawn, during the morning watch, the Lord looked down on the Egyptian army from the fiery cloud. He threw the entire Egyptian force into wild panic and confusion. Flashes of divine fire, thunder, and terror broke their discipline and threw their lines into disorder.

God made the chariot wheels break off or get stuck in the sea bed, making it nearly impossible to drive. The Egyptians panicked and shouted that they must run away, because the Lord was fighting for Israel against them. By the time they admitted that God was fighting them, their chance to escape was gone.

Once the Israelites had crossed, the Lord told Moses to stretch his hand out over the sea once more. This command instructed the held-back waters to collapse over the trapped Egyptian chariots and riders. The very sea that offered safe passage to Israel was about to bring judgment on their enemies.

Moses stretched his hand over the water, and at daybreak the sea rushed back to its normal place with violent force. The Egyptians tried to turn and run against the incoming surge, but the Lord swept them into the crashing waves. Human armies and weapons could not withstand the returning tide.

The waters crashed together and completely buried all the chariots, horsemen, and soldiers that had entered the sea bed. Pharaoh's entire pursuing army was wiped out, leaving not a single soldier alive. God completely broke Egypt's military might so they could never pursue Israel again.

While the Egyptian army drowned, the Israelites walked through on dry land with walls of water on each side. The text repeats this wonder to emphasize the great difference between those who trust God and those who fight Him. Faith led Israel to life, while pride led Egypt to destruction.

On that memorable day, the Lord completely rescued Israel from Egyptian oppression, and the people saw the bodies of their pursuers on the shore. Seeing their former masters dead gave them unmistakable proof that their slavery was truly finished. God brought an end to centuries of hardship with one complete victory.

When Israel saw the great power the Lord used against Egypt, the people were filled with deep reverent awe toward God. They placed their trust in the Lord and believed in Moses as His true servant. Seeing God's faithfulness built their confidence as they began their long march toward the promised land.
